activity.title: Be the team that gets on the plane and makes sh*t happen. We recently launched Soar in iMessage and adoption has been hard to ignore. At the same time, I keep noticing more and more companies building agents for iMessage. It's clearly a growing ecosystem, but there's no easy way to discover them. So I built the iMessage Agent Store to fix that. Last Friday I talked to Elliott Potter about it. By Monday, he and Patrick Sullivan were at our offsite in Mexico City. Thrilled to launch the Agent Store together 🚀 A marketplace of AI agents you can text. Go text Soar!

Introducing the Agent Store: one place to discover agents you can text. No downloads, no new apps, just open Messages. Built with our friend Stanley Virgint at Soar , the Agent Store is a marketplace where anyone can discover and interact with conversational agents like Soar, Tomo, and Noscroll in one place.

I made an App Store for iMessage agents. Every week lately I've noticed another AI agent you can text in iMessage. After launching Soar in iMessage, I realized there wasn't a single place to discover what else was out there, and the landscape is growing exponentially. So here it is. Who am I missing? Tag the best AI agents to have in your iMessage below 👇 Link to website in the comments!

I just won at TreeHacks this weekend. I wasn't originally going, but decided to check their team formation Slack at 11 PM Friday night. I was blessed enough to meet ethan ⌘ and Pranav Karra , who were working on building a generic voice agent. We ended up hopping on a Google Meet and working online for 6 straight hours. We decided to make our agent call various businesses and negotiate for better deals and named it Kiru. Some highlights of our time there: At around 3:52 AM, we had a local database getting generated, and I was trying to fix why we couldn't delete chats on our frontend. It took me around 3 crashouts and a few laughs to figure out that in one of our Python files, there was a function that was deeply embedded into our code that spawned this local SQLite DB. At 1:05 PM, we met Stanley Virgint , pitching to him about Kiru. He built Soar, a travel agent that reimagines traveling. At 4:05 PM, we heard our name being called out for the 2nd place prize for the Bright Data track. This entire experience genuinely couldn't have been done without the support of ethan ⌘ and Pranav Karra . Being a freshman here was crazy; it seemed everyone around me founded a startup, gotten funded, and had a ton of experience. I also can't thank Bright Data and the The Bright Initiative by Bright Data enough for the prize. Their new tools laid the foundation for our entire product. Also, thanks so much to Sunday Ajak for the photos taken for the entirety of TreeHacks. This experience genuinely was one that I will remember for the rest of my life. Ignoring technical skills for a second, this experience really showed me the importance of social skills being a computer science major. In judging, in general conversations, talking to sponsors, one thing that everyone had a strong skillset in was communication. I learned a lot from hearing conversations, seeing ethan ⌘ pitch, and talking to all the judges. And that is a wrap on TreeHacks 2026. I hope to be there next year!

i met ethan ⌘ on the treehacks slack. turned out i also knew his work from twitter. we started working on a basic idea of a voice agent when we came across Jayanth Sidamsety . > we were on a 6 hour google meet working over night. > Jay drove over in the morning. > we named the agent kiru > benchmarking different llms for the agent (both on dgx spark and api) > adding tooling so it can do more things > 9 am ish on satuday - first version is live and it could call us > slow as hell, very robotic > we found a better voice, and streamed every part of the pipeline so its realtime > realized we might need a cloud database > losing our mind because the local database keeps coming back even after force deleting everything (this was hilarious) > called a bunch of businesses > got suspended from our telephony provider twilio > rushed to create a new account and rewire the backend > realized we cant use our local system at the demos > deployed backend to gcp asap > made everything public > designed a goated website > recorded a demo 10min before submission deadline > people came upto our demo and loved the design, didnt care about the agent so much, many thought it was just simulated data > we ask them "do you want us to call you?" > they talk to kiru > now theyre interested, and stay and talk with us for 10 minutes about the entire stack and connect with us > realize our demo is goated because we can just call everyone coming to our table > we win # 2 on Bright Data Track twas fun. Sunday Ajak thanks for taking our pictures.

I am proud to share that this past weekend, my partner Adhvaidh Sunny and I won Cal Hacks 12.0, Best Use of ElevenLabs! This was my first collegiate hackathon, and it also happened to be the biggest one in the world, with over 3,600 students participating. We built an AI that can understand natural voice commands, read what’s on your screen, and handle multi-step actions across different apps automatically, basically a system that executes whatever you say, from playing music to scheduling meetings, all in one flow. (Imagine Jarvis from Iron Man) I want to give a huge thank you to Cal Hacks for hosting such an incredible event and ElevenLabs for choosing me and my partner. It was an amazing experience all around!

Just took 3rd place at the OpenAI × Start2 × Zendesk Hackathon at the Hanwha AI Center. How? Here's the explanation: Most AI support tools break the moment someone can't hand them a clean sentence. We spent a weekend building one that doesn't need the sentence at all. We call it Wordless. Two million Americans live with aphasia. They understand everything you say to them, they just can't always retrieve the words to say back what's wrong. Ask someone mid-anomia to describe a billing error and you might get a bunch of random words: "order… wrong… the thing… help." Every support agent on the market reads that, grabs the nearest-sounding help article, and closes the ticket confidently wrong. Wordless doesn't ask the person to explain. It figures it out. The moment a request comes in, it reads the customer's actual account - recent charges, orders, past tickets - and flags what's most likely broken. Two identical charges thirty seconds apart? That's the problem, and no one had to type the word "duplicate." Whatever fragment the person can offer gets matched by meaning, not spelling, so "the boily thing" still lands on their kettle order. Then it lays out the top few guesses as big tap-to-confirm cards. Four words in, one tap out. Under the hood: Composio for the account reads, Octen for the semantic matching, Codex generating the interface live, Zendesk closing the loop. We were the only high school team there, and it was our first hackathon - so hearing our name called for one of 5 selected presentation slots, then again for 3rd place, was not something we saw coming. Huge thanks to Nick Lum , founder of BeeLine Reader, who spent real time speaking to us about his experiences and sharpening how we thought about the whole thing. Grateful for that. And to my teammates Avinash Amanchi , Akshat Agarwal and Rushil Baindla - this was all of us. Thanks to OpenAI , Composio , Octen AI , Zendesk , and Start2 Group for hosting such a great event. More coming.

Almanac (YC S26) is building the shared knowledge layer for your team’s coding agents. We’re proud to be part of Y Combinator Summer 2026 batch. Coding agents can write more code than ever, but every new session starts from zero. Engineers spend hundreds of hours re-explaining product requirements, implementation decisions, architecture, and past incidents. Agents repeat investigations, make decisions that contradict earlier work, and rediscover knowledge the company already has. That knowledge exists, but it is scattered across Slack , Linear , GitHub , documentation, and thousands of AI conversations. The result is more time spent prompting, reviewing, and correcting work that should have been right the first time. Almanac turns that scattered knowledge into a cited, self-updating wiki. Before making changes, agents search Almanac for the relevant requirements, decisions, implementation history, and lessons from past incidents. Every agent works from the same shared context, without engineers repeatedly explaining the codebase. Keep every coding agent on your team on the same page.
